Dynamic ST-T change with pain is more specific
Flat or downsloping ST depression above 0.1 mV for over 0.08 s
Nondiagnostic if under 85% of predicted maximal heart rate
A negative test does not exclude CAD
Use when resting ECG is abnormal or patient cannot exercise
Initial test under age 65 with intermediate or high probability
ST depression of 0.2 mV or more, or SBP fall over 10 mmHg
{{hy:Low workload ischaemia or EF below 0.40 marks high risk}}
Luminal narrowing over 70% significant without FFR
Gold standard; FFR clarifies equivocal lesions
Angina walking 1 to 2 blocks or one flight of stairs
Class IV: angina with any activity or at rest

valueTables.footnote: Stress ECG sensitivity differs: Merck (2026) gives 46 to 68%, Harrison 22e about 75%. Harrison notes flow reserve falls at about 50% narrowing; Merck treats over 70% as significant on angiography.

Ejection murmur; angina from LV hypertrophy without CAD
Rest pain, often at night, transient ST elevation
Ambulatory ECG or provocation at angiography
Ischaemic pain without epicardial obstruction, commoner in women
Trial of acid suppression or endoscopy

cells.text: Acute angina; repeat every 4 to 5 minutes up to 3 doses
DAPT with a P2Y12 inhibitor usually 12 months after PCI
Add ezetimibe or PCSK9 inhibitor if needed
{{hy:First line with LVEF 50% or less or prior MI}}
Titrate to heart rate and tolerance
Beta-blocker not tolerated or symptoms persist
Avoid short-acting nifedipine alone; amlodipine if LV dysfunction
Needs a nitrate-free interval to avoid tolerance
Ranolazine prolongs QT; ivabradine for sinus rate 70/min or more
CCS class III or IV on medical therapy, high-risk noninvasive test, sudden death survivor, sustained VT
Persistent angina despite therapy or high-risk anatomy
CABG favoured in diabetes with multivessel disease and in left main disease
Smoking cessation, BP below 130/80, exercise, vaccination
